parent.name: Italian Game
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 aiming at f7 and prepares to take the centre with c3 and d4 or, more quietly, d3 (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads: 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's set-up, 3...Nf6 (Two Knights) invites sharper play, and 3...Be7 (Hungarian) is passive and solid (own understanding for the last). Today's main practical line is the Giuoco Pianissimo with c3, d3 and slow manoeuvring, which became fashionable in the 1980s-2000s and again in the 21st century as a way to avoid the Berlin (s1). The older 4.c3 and d4 lines and the Evans Gambit are sharper (s1). It is fundamentally sound with modest winning chances (s1). It is described as accessible to beginners yet used by Giri, So and Vachier-Lagrave (s3).

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: English Opening
parent.overview: White opens with the c-pawn to contest d5 from the wing, keeping the e4, d4, g3 and b3 options open until Black reveals a set-up. It is a flexible, hypermodern, mostly positional opening: not as sharp as 1.e4 or 1.d4, with the character decided by Black's reply and by transpositions into the Queen's Gambit, Réti or King's Indian. Principal branches are the Reversed Sicilian (1...e5, with an extra tempo for White), the Symmetrical (1...c5, often with a Maroczy bind) and the Anglo-Indian (1...Nf6 and 1...e6/...g6 transpositions). White typically plays Nc3, g3 and Bg2, and expands on the queenside with Rb1 and b4, or takes the classical centre with e4. The database root is a crossroads; its most-played continuations are transpositions to QGD (1.c4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4), the King's Indian and the Réti.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Symmetrical Variation
parent.overview: This is a crossroads reached by symmetrical knight development: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6. Nothing is committed in the centre; the character is decided by White's third move. 3.c4 transposes to Queen's Gambit structures (QGD, Slav, Semi-Slav, QGA) and is by far the most played continuation in the database; 3.g3 gives the Pseudo-Catalan (a Catalan-style fianchetto); 3.e3 with Bd3 and c3 is the Colle; 3.Bf4 or 2.Bf4 is the London; 3.c3 is a flexible quiet set-up. Wikipedia and ChessBase describe the non-c4 lines as closed-centre system play with simple development plans and little theory. Black is generally free to develop logically (...e6, ...c5 or ...c6, ...Bf5/Bg4).

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Normal Defense
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: Black answers 3.Nc3 with the natural 3...Nf6, defending d5 and eyeing e4. This is a crossroads in which White chooses between 4.Bg5 (the pin and the classical Orthodox, Lasker, Tartakower and Cambridge Springs lines), 4.cxd5 (the Exchange and Carlsbad structure, dominant at 2500 level) and 4.Nf3, which keeps options open and lets Black pick a QGD, Ragozin (...Bb4) or Semi-Slav (...c6) set-up (s1, s4). The QGD systems are solid with straightforward plans: ...Nf6, ...Be7, ...O-O against most lines, and the ...c5 break (s2). White's typical plans are the minority attack and e4 expansion (s1). The Semi-Slav moves 4.Nf3 c6 5.Bg5 (Botvinnik) are outside the QGD in character, very forcing (s4). The root as a whole is the Orthodox QGD family and its transpositions. The site's current text for this root is a copy of the parent QGD text.

parent.name: Slav Defense
parent.overview: Black supports d5 with ...c6 so that the centre is held by pawns while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out (usually to f5 or g4) before ...e6. The root is a crossroads: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Black chooses the Pure Slav with ...dxc4 (active bishop, ...e5/...c5 breaks), the Semi-Slav with ...e6 (c6-d5-e6 triangle, theory-heavy and often sharp: Meran, Botvinnik, Anti-Meran), or the Chebanenko ...a6. White can also play the Exchange (cxd5 cxd5), a symmetrical structure with queenside minority attack ideas that has a drawish reputation, or quiet systems with 3.e3 or 3.Bf4. The Slav is played by many world champions (Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand, Kramnik) and is regarded as sound; sources treat it as solid with room for counterplay rather than a forced-draw defence.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6 5. Nf3
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.
